A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work with the same title, authors, and central experiments. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding equations, tables, figures, and allocation matrices can be matched despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v2 reports original LLM hiring simulations, intervention experiments, and supplementary analyses in Sections 4–5 and the appendices. The separately attributed human baseline is not the sole empirical evidence.

after.justification: v4 retains original LLM experiments and adds newer-model evaluations, bandit comparisons, controlled ablations, and forced-failure continuation results.

M1.justification: v4 introduces a tested context-summary inference variant: demographic-job counts and empirical success rates replace the full dialogue history (Section 5.1, Appendix A.3). This extends the intervention procedures; the core hiring paradigm and diversity-bonus mechanism remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v4 adds an abstract bandit scenario without social or occupational semantics and feedback-altered scenarios, including forced-failure continuations. These extend the simulated decision conditions within the existing allocation task family. Hiring, refugee resettlement, conscription, and real-demographic scenarios are retained.

E2.justification: v4 adds evaluated Thompson-sampling and UCB1 baselines, substantially broadening comparison beyond humans and random assignment (Section 4.1, Appendix E). Primary model comparisons also add GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash. The matched p=0.1 human reference displayed in v2 Figure 5 is absent from the replacement v4 Table 2.

E3.justification: The original 40-round, 30-run primary design remains, but v4 adds substantial control protocols: compressed histories, temperature zero, five fixed job trajectories with ten trials each, and removal of outcome feedback and bonus wording. Its new continuation experiment imposes ten failed rounds per job quadrant and measures first deviation, recording 11 when none occurs. The abstract task additionally evaluates allocation entropy.

E4.justification: v4 adds analyses testing context accumulation, semantic framing, sampling variance, job-order variance, feedback dependence, and resistance to renewed exploration (Sections 5.1–5.2, Appendices G and J). Appendix E also examines UCB1 exploration-coefficient sensitivity. Existing ReAct, unequal-success-rate, real-demographic, and diversity-tradeoff analyses are retained under different appendix labels.

E5.justification: v2 already reports repeated runs and 95% confidence intervals. v4 newly states that significance testing accounts for a Benjamini-Hochberg correction at alpha=0.05 and adds uncertainty entries for GASI controls. The primary run count remains 30; the new correction disclosure does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results for newer models, bandit baselines, and mechanistic controls. Examples include GASI values of 0.63, 0.61, and 0.61 for GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash, and Thompson-sampling SI=0.61 (Table 1, Appendix E). Matched allocation matrices and many older results remain unchanged. v4 Table 2 reports random-assignment SI=0.291, whereas v2 reports 0.25 and v4's main results and Table 3 retain 0.25; this discrepancy is unexplained.

T1.justification: Appendix J adds brief probabilistic reasoning linking consecutive failures to probabilities of 10^-1 through 10^-5 and arguing that the required failure sequence bounds natural unlearning likelihood. The metric definitions and Appendix B's SI–mutual-information lemma and proof are unchanged.

C1.justification: The central claims about novel bias formation, greater stratification in stronger models, and the effectiveness of explicit diversity incentives remain. v4 adds a concluding claim that models only begin unlearning after exceedingly unlikely outcome sequences (Discussion, Appendix J), extending the paper's message about resistance to correction.

C2.justification: v4 develops a more specific mechanism account: outcome feedback principally drives stochasticity, semantic framing shapes allocation patterns, and accumulated context alone does not explain stratification. It also interprets forced-failure responses through anchoring while acknowledging that first deviation does not guarantee unlearning. The diversity-versus-success limitation already present in v2 Appendix G is retained in v4 Appendix K.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-repository link on the title page and exact templates for the abstract bandit and compressed-summary experiments (Appendices A.2–A.3), including summary construction and omission of groups with no hires. It also documents baseline coefficients and continuation handling. Existing prompting and hyperparameter information is largely retained.

R1.justification: The distinction between pretrained stereotypes and emergent interaction-driven biases remains the central positioning. v4 adds connections and citations concerning statistical discrimination, classical bandit policies, anchoring, and long-context failures. It removes the standalone HELM leaderboard and Sutton–Barto references; publication and author-name updates elsewhere concern retained works.

P1.justification: The overall six-section narrative remains, with copyediting and focused revisions to the introduction and discussion. Model settings move from Section 4.1 to 3.3, several appendices are reordered, acknowledgments are added, and the Ethics Statement becomes an Impact Statement with essentially the same content.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a two-column conference layout and extensively revises displays. Figure 3 gains BGD alongside SI, v2 Figure 5 becomes v4 Table 2, and v2 Figure 6's two feature-ablation panels merge into v4 Figure 5 with corrected feature labels. Table 1 expands and new control tables appear. Existing appendix allocation matrices are reflowed without changing their numerical contents.

improvement.justification: v2 supported emergence mainly through stochastic assignments and initial-association tests. v4 substantially strengthens the central mechanism analysis with classical bandit comparisons and targeted controls for sampling, job order, feedback, context length, and semantic framing. Added prompts and a code link improve reproducibility information. Some conclusions remain overstated—the forced-failure probe measures first deviation, not completed unlearning—and Table 2 introduces an inconsistent random baseline, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in supporting evidence.
